adversary.title: Almost every messenger encrypts today. What matters is whether that encryption will also hold against a future quantum computer.
paragraphs: Methods common today rest on mathematical problems a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve. Nobody knows when such machines will exist — but keeping intercepted data until they do is already common practice.
Silvra therefore combines classical cryptography with ML-⁠KEM, the method standardised in 2024 by the US standards institute NIST. Both together, not one alone: if one breaks, the other still holds.
adversary.highlight: The keys live only on your devices. We cannot read the content of your chats — not even if a government asks. What our servers can read includes posts in the Updates feed, your email address, your status, your signed-in devices, your group memberships and the connection data needed for delivery.

helix.subtitle: A layer-1 blockchain secured by NIST-standardised post-quantum cryptography — every signature ML-⁠DSA-⁠65, from the very first block.

live.title: The chain, block by block.
live.lead: Every new block shows up here as soon as the public node reports it — with its height, hash and transactions. A click opens it in the explorer.

intro.title: Not retrofitted. Built from the ground up.
intro.body: Instead of migrating an existing chain to post-quantum later, Helix is designed for it from the first line of code: ML-⁠DSA-⁠65 on every transaction, block and validator vote — no transition period, no classical signature schemes to swap out down the line.

why.title: What existing blockchains leave open.
why.lead: Six problems Helix does not leave for later, but has solved since its first line of code.

rows.problem: A large quantum computer can break ECDSA and Ed25519 signatures
rows.helix: ML-⁠DSA-⁠65 (NIST FIPS 204) on every transaction, block and vote

rows.problem: Stake buys voting power without limit
rows.helix: Each validator’s voting power capped at 1% of total stake

rows.problem: Hex addresses; a lost key is lost for good
rows.helix: alice.hlx names and recovery through guardians

rows.problem: No plan for the next cryptographic migration
rows.helix: The signature scheme is versioned in every transaction

rows.problem: Zero-knowledge proofs resting on elliptic curves (SNARKs)
A contract that runs forever stalls the chain
rows.helix: WASM VM, fuel-metered per transaction and per block, no floating point

chain.title: Eight decisions, block by block
chain.lead: What the protocol is made of — and where to read it in the code.

features.title: ML-⁠DSA-⁠65 everywhere
features.body: Every transaction, every block, every validator vote. No classical scheme with a migration plan attached.

features.title: Crypto agility built in
features.body: The signature scheme is versioned in every transaction; SLH-⁠DSA (FIPS 205) stands by as a hash-based reserve.

features.title: Final in about two seconds
features.body: Tendermint-style BFT consensus: a block stands once more than two thirds of the vote is behind it — and, as long as less than a third of the vote is faulty, is never reverted.

features.title: Voting power capped
features.body: Each validator’s voting power is capped at 1% of total stake — capital alone buys no majority. That only means at most 1% of the vote once there are 100 validators; today the set is far smaller.

features.title: Names and recovery
features.body: alice.hlx instead of a hex address — and social recovery through guardians when a key is lost.

features.title: WASM contracts without reentrancy
features.body: Fuel-metered, no floating point, no calls between contracts: the best-known attack surface simply is not there.

features.title: ZK-STARKs
features.body: Zero-knowledge proofs built on hashes alone — no elliptic curves for a quantum computer to break.

features.title: Upgrades by governance
features.body: Protocol changes are voted on-chain and activate at a height announced in advance. No more resets since 1.0.0.

supply.title: Capped, traceable, with a disclosed genesis allocation.
supply.lead: Every number is in the code. More than 99% of all HLX only come into being by producing blocks.
supply.chartTitle: HLX supply over time — upper bound, before burned fees
supply.aria: Line chart: HLX supply rises from 161,000 at genesis to about 31.7 million after 30 years, as the block reward halves every year. The hard cap is 33 million. Use the arrow keys to pick a year.
supply.caption: Computed from the protocol parameters: 1 HLX per block, halved every 15,768,000 blocks (≈ 1 year at 2 s). Burned fees are not subtracted. Issuance approaches about 31.7M HLX; the 33M cap sits above it and is fixed in code.

honesty.title: A young network with known limits.

items.title: The validator set is still small
items.body: With n validators the network survives ⌊(n−1)/3⌋ failures: four survive one, seven survive two — three or fewer survive none. When too many are missing, the chain stops and waits; it does not fork. Active right now: {{validators}}.

items.title: HLX is not an investment
items.body: Since 1.0.0 nothing is reset any more. That does not mean HLX is worth anything — and we do not claim it is.

items.title: The transport uses classical encryption
items.body: Nodes connect over libp2p Noise (X25519). What they exchange is public and ML-⁠DSA-signed: a quantum computer could read along but forge nothing.

items.title: Consensus at scale: shown in tests, not yet in production
items.body: Vote locking, re-proposals and double-sign detection are exercised in fault-injection and chaos tests — including with a third of all messages lost, with no fork. The live network is still small.

items.title: Reviewed continuously from an attacker’s point of view — AI-assisted
items.body: The review runs alongside development with Claude (Anthropic), as the README describes. Every finding is first reproduced as a test, then fixed; as a cross-check, reverting the fix must make the test fail again. No independent external audit has been published so far.

honesty.highlight: We would rather say this up front than have to explain it afterwards.

items.q: Do I need my own node?
items.a: No. The wallet and the command line talk to the public network with no setup. A node of your own is worth it if you want to validate or verify the chain independently.

items.q: How do I become a validator?
items.a: With at least 10,000 HLX staked and a running node — from the command line or in one click from the desktop wallet, behind NAT or a proxy too. The guide is in the documentation under “Running a Node”.

items.q: Can I take part without running a node?
items.a: Yes, by delegating: you put your stake behind a validator and receive a share of its earnings, less commission (10% by default, at most 50%).

items.q: What happens when validators go down?
items.a: With n validators the network survives ⌊(n−1)/3⌋ failures. With more missing, the chain stops and waits — it does not fork. A validator that stops signing is suspended for a while. Under protocol 1, active today, that costs no stake; from protocol 2, once stakers vote it in, it does.
A base fee per byte, burned in full, plus a tip for the validator. The base fee follows demand (at most ±12.5% per block); the wallet never pays more than 1 HLX on its own.
No. The network is young, and nothing here promises it is worth anything.

mission.title: What is intercepted today can be read later
mission.subtitle: We build digital infrastructure prepared for quantum computers — originating in Europe.

approach.statement: Post-quantum cryptography from the start — built in while a project is young enough to do so without breaking anything.
paragraphs: Key exchange and signatures on today’s internet mostly rest on RSA or elliptic curves. A sufficiently large quantum computer breaks both; nobody knows when one will exist.
That is why, wherever we have the choice, we rely on the schemes the US standards institute NIST standardised in 2024: ML-⁠KEM (FIPS 203), ML-⁠DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-⁠DSA (FIPS 205).
The second motive: Europe should have alternatives of its own — software developed here, subject to European law and actually usable day to day.

accessibility.title: Accessibility statement
accessibility.subtitle: This site should work for everyone — by keyboard, with a screen reader, magnified or without any animation at all.

sections.title: Aim
sections.body: We build silvra.net to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, conformance level AA. This statement covers silvra.net and all its pages; the Helix Explorer and outside services such as Google Play or GitHub are not part of it.

sections.title: Compliance status
sections.body: By our checks, silvra.net complies with WCAG 2.2 AA; we currently know of no deviation from level AA. If you find one, please report it — how is described below.

sections.title: How the site meets it
items: A switch “Pause motion and live values” in the header stops every animation and every self-updating number; the operating system’s “reduce motion” setting is honoured as well.
Everything can be reached by keyboard, focus is always visible and every page starts with a “Skip to content” link. On the home page, ← and → choose a sector.
Text reaches a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, in the light and the dark theme.
Status is never conveyed by colour alone, always with a symbol and a word as well.
The encrypted-looking characters behind the home page and the messenger page are decoration and hidden from screen readers; what they show is said in the text.
Every page is delivered as finished HTML and readable without JavaScript; headings, landmarks and language are marked up.
The site can be zoomed to 400% and used down to 320 pixels wide without scrolling sideways.

sections.title: How we check
sections.body: Before releases we check every page in the light and dark theme, at desktop and phone width, with axe-core against WCAG 2.2 A and AA — including contrast and target size — and test keyboard operation, zoom up to 400% and the motion switch. Last check: 14 October 2026.

sections.title: Beyond this
sections.body: What goes beyond level AA or falls outside this statement:
items: There is currently no content in Easy Read or in sign language.
The Helix Explorer is a separate application with a very dense display; it is not covered by this statement.
